lesson_title: How Sorghum Saves Water for Grain Filling

primary_source.title: Stay-green alleles individually enhance grain yield in sorghum under drought by modifying canopy development and water uptake patterns
primary_source.publication_date_note: First published online; volume 203, issue 3, pages 817–830
primary_source.access_note: Publisher full text, including Materials and Methods, Results, Discussion, Tables 1–3, and figure captions, inspected. The page labels the paper Free Access; no Creative Commons license verified for this primary article.

supporting_research_source.title: Drought adaptation of stay-green sorghum is associated with canopy development, leaf anatomy, root growth, and water uptake
supporting_research_source.role: Supporting original research article from the same research group, explicitly distinguished in the narration. Its openly licensed explanations and reporting of the related experiments support expanded educational discussion; it does not replace the New Phytologist anchor.

sourced_facts.claim: Seven experiments and fourteen managed environments formed the main study.
The authors used four near-isogenic RTx7000 lines containing individual Stg1, Stg2, Stg3, or Stg4 regions from BTx642.
sourced_facts.locator: Materials and Methods, Generation of RTx7000 NILs; companion Materials and methods, Construction of RTx7000 NILs

sourced_facts.claim: In WAR05FLD low-water/high-density plots, Stg1 used 139 versus 172 mm before anthesis and 197 versus 145 mm afterward.
sourced_facts.locator: Results, Stg QTLs affected crop water use before and after flowering; Figure 7; companion temporal water-use discussion

sourced_facts.claim: The main paper links stay-green regions to a smaller canopy at flowering and better drought yield, with different effects among regions.
sourced_facts.locator: Results, Tables 2–3; companion Results and discussion

sourced_facts.claim: Greater uptake suggested a root contribution; the main study did not directly demonstrate deeper Stg1 roots.
sourced_facts.locator: Discussion, Impact of canopy development on grain yield under drought via water availability and drought adaptation; companion Stg loci modify root architecture and spatial water extraction patterns
sourced_facts.evidence_type: Boundary between measured result and proposed mechanism

sourced_facts.claim: Water treatments in the Warwick field trials occupied separate blocks because of rain-shelter constraints.
sourced_facts.locator: Materials and Methods, Field experiments; companion Field experiments

interpretive_limits: A QTL is a genomic region, not necessarily one identified causal gene.
The primary NIL comparisons use the RTx7000 genetic background and cannot establish identical effects in all sorghum varieties.
The primary study provides evidence for canopy and water-use changes; a unique architectural root cause was not identified.
Drought-yield improvements were not statistically significant in every individual comparison.
No consistent irrigated yield penalty does not mean there was no penalty in any irrigated treatment.
Field water depletion is not a direct measurement of a complete root architecture.
The lesson does not treat water-flow simulations as automatically predicting grain yield.

modelling_relevance.status: Proposed application by lesson author, not performed in the cited sorghum studies
modelling_relevance.proposal: Separate canopy-demand, root-architecture, and hydraulic-property changes before testing their combination. Compare both timing and depth-resolved soil water, and check against independent plant observations.
